31.event_title: The Cadbury brothers move their works to Bournville
31.event: In 1861 the brothers George and Richard Cadbury took over their father's failing cocoa business, and in 1879 they moved their factory four miles out of industrial Birmingham to a rural site they named Bournville. There they introduced a private social security programme and working conditions far in advance of their time, and from 1893 George Cadbury built a model village of houses with large gardens, which he handed to the Bournville Village Trust in 1900. The firm grew into the highly prosperous Cadbury Brothers company, and Bournville became a model for later garden cities and suburbs.
31.explanation: The Cadburys showed that a business run on ethical principles could become both rich and widely respected, its decent treatment of workers adding to rather than draining its success.
31.tie_back: The kural says virtue yields both honour and prosperity, and the Cadburys' firm gained both the wealth and the lasting good name that their humane practices earned.
31._accuracy_note: A clear case of conduct that brought both honour and wealth, though the kural's sirappu also carries a spiritual sense of liberation that no business history can show.

32.event_title: The collapse of Charles Ponzi's scheme
32.event: In late 1919 Charles Ponzi, an Italian immigrant, opened a business in Boston promising investors a 50 percent return in 45 days from trading international postal reply coupons. In fact he paid earlier investors with money taken from later ones, and he became very rich within months. After journalists at the Boston Post investigated, the scheme collapsed in August 1920; Ponzi was arrested, convicted of mail fraud and imprisoned, several banks failed in the aftermath, and he was later deported to Italy, dying in poverty in Brazil in 1949.
32.explanation: Ponzi's name became the standard term for this kind of fraud, and his rapid rise and total fall is one of the best-known warnings about wealth built on deceit.
32.tie_back: The kural says there is no greater ruin than forgetting virtue, and Ponzi's fortune, built by setting honesty aside, ended in disgrace, prison and poverty.
32._accuracy_note: Illustrates the ruin that follows abandoning virtue well, though Ponzi's fraud was deliberate rather than the forgetful lapse the commentators stress.

33.event_title: Chiune Sugihara issues transit visas to refugees
33.event: In the summer of 1940 Chiune Sugihara, Japan's consul in Kaunas, was approached by Jewish refugees from Poland who needed Japanese transit visas to escape Europe. Although many applicants did not meet the conditions his Foreign Ministry required, he kept issuing visas until his consulate closed, stamping some passports himself and enlisting helpers when time ran short, and by the time he left Lithuania he had issued visas to more than 2,000 people. Yad Vashem recognised him as Righteous Among the Nations in 1984.
33.explanation: Sugihara used the one tool his position gave him, his consular stamp, as fully and as long as he could, and thousands of people escaped because of it.
33.tie_back: The kural urges doing good by whatever means one has, without letting up, wherever good can reach, and Sugihara kept writing visas with the means of his office until the very last day it was open.
33._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's call for unceasing good done with whatever means are at hand.

34.event_title: Wilhelm Röntgen declines to patent X-rays
34.event: After discovering X-rays at Würzburg in November 1895, the physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen chose not to take out a patent on his discovery, because he felt his work should benefit everyone. He rejected an offered title of nobility and offers from industry to market the rays, and when he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 he donated the prize money to the University of Würzburg.
34.explanation: Röntgen's quiet refusals let X-ray imaging spread rapidly through medicine while he himself sought neither profit nor rank from it.
34.tie_back: The kural says virtue lies wholly in a mind free of stain and that the rest is noise and show, and Röntgen turned away both profit and titles, keeping his discovery free of private gain.
34._accuracy_note: Shows purity of motive over outward reward, but the kural's sharp contrast between inner stainlessness and outward religious display is only partly reflected.

35.event_title: Nelson Mandela wears the Springbok jersey at the Rugby World Cup final
35.event: Nelson Mandela, imprisoned from 1962 until his release in 1990 and elected South Africa's president in 1994, attended the 1995 Rugby World Cup final between South Africa and New Zealand. Before the match he walked into the Springbok changing room wearing a Springbok jersey with captain Francois Pienaar's number six, and after South Africa's victory he presented the trophy to Pienaar on the field while wearing it. The Nelson Mandela Foundation describes the moment as an enduring symbol of the democratic government's approach to reconciliation and nation-building.
35.explanation: Mandela embraced a sporting symbol cherished by many white South Africans, choosing reconciliation over resentment after decades of imprisonment under apartheid.
35.tie_back: The kural defines virtue as conduct that steadily keeps clear of envy, greed, anger and harsh words, and Mandela's public gesture of goodwill toward former opponents shows anger and bitterness set aside.
35._accuracy_note: A strong public example of freedom from anger and harsh speech, though one occasion cannot show the steady lifelong conduct the kural describes.

36.place: St. John's, Newfoundland, to Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada
36.event: Terry Fox, who had lost his right leg to cancer at 18, set out from St. John's on 12 April 1980 to run across Canada and raise money for cancer research, covering 5,373 kilometres in 143 days, nearly a marathon a day. He was forced to stop near Thunder Bay on 1 September 1980 when his cancer returned, and he died on 28 June 1981. Before his death his goal of one dollar for every Canadian had been reached, and the annual Terry Fox Run held in his name has since raised hundreds of millions of dollars for cancer research.
36.explanation: Fox did not wait for a better time to act; he ran while he could, and the good he began has continued long after his death.
36.tie_back: The kural warns against saying we will do good later and calls virtue the companion that does not perish when we perish, and Fox's run, made in the time he had, lives on in the yearly runs and research funded in his name.
36._accuracy_note: Closely fits the urgency of doing good now and the good that outlasts the doer, though the kural's companion is meant in a karmic sense beyond earthly legacy.

37.event_title: Charles Booth maps London's wealth and poverty street by street
37.event: Charles Booth, a successful businessman who doubted a claim that a quarter of Londoners lived in extreme poverty, funded and led a street-by-street inquiry into living conditions from 1886. In 1889 he published the first of his Descriptive Maps of London Poverty, colouring every residential street from yellow for the wealthy to black for the poorest, so that rich and poor streets could be seen side by side. His survey found that about 30.7 percent of Londoners lived in poverty, more than he had expected.
37.explanation: Booth's maps made the gulf between fortunes in one city visible at a glance, and they became a founding example of social mapping.
37.tie_back: The kural says no argument is needed because the difference in fortunes can simply be seen, as between palanquin-bearer and rider, and Booth's coloured streets let anyone see such differences for themselves.
37._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows unequal fortunes made directly visible, but the kural's claim that these differences are the fruit of past virtue is a karmic teaching that no historical event can demonstrate, and Booth's maps imply nothing of the kind.

38.event_title: Florence Nightingale's night rounds at Scutari
38.event: Florence Nightingale reached the British army's military hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War in late 1854 with a party of nurses. She organised cleaning, food kitchens and laundries, wrote letters home for soldiers and set up reading rooms, and in the evenings she went through the wards carrying a lamp to tend patients; a paper lantern she used on these rounds is now in the National Army Museum. She remained at Scutari until 1856, and she became known as the Lady with the Lamp, a name later fixed in Longfellow's poem Santa Filomena.
38.explanation: Nightingale's daily and nightly care helped transform nursing into a respected profession and set standards for modern hospital care.
38.tie_back: The kural praises doing good without letting a single day fall away empty, and Nightingale's work, continued even through the nights, filled every day she spent at Scutari.
38._accuracy_note: Illustrates the daily, unbroken practice of good well, but the kural's promise that such practice blocks rebirth is a spiritual claim beyond history.

39.event_title: Ben Johnson is stripped of his Olympic gold medal
39.event: On 24 September 1988 the Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson won the 100 metres at the Seoul Olympics in a world-record 9.79 seconds. Three days later he tested positive for the steroid stanozolol, and the International Olympic Committee stripped him of the gold medal and awarded it to the runner-up, Carl Lewis. Johnson, celebrated as the world's fastest man one day, became a byword for cheating in sport.
39.explanation: The episode is one of the most famous reversals in sporting history and a lasting lesson that victory gained by breaking the rules brings disgrace rather than glory.
39.tie_back: The kural says only what comes by way of virtue is true joy, while everything else is outside joy and brings no honour, and Johnson's triumph, won by forbidden means, was taken away within days and left only dishonour.
39._accuracy_note: A vivid case of gain won outside virtue yielding neither lasting joy nor honour, matching both halves of the kural.

40.event_title: Frances Kelsey refuses to approve thalidomide
40.event: In 1960, during her first month as a medical officer at the US Food and Drug Administration, Frances Oldham Kelsey was assigned the application to market thalidomide, a sleeping pill already sold in many countries. Despite constant pressure from the company, she refused to approve it until she had scientifically reliable evidence of its safety. About a year later researchers linked the drug to severe birth defects in thousands of babies in other countries; thalidomide was never marketed in the United States, and in 1962 President Kennedy gave Kelsey the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service.
40.explanation: By doing exactly what her duty required and refusing what would have been blameworthy, Kelsey prevented a tragedy in her country and helped bring about stronger drug laws.
40.tie_back: The kural says what ought to be done is virtue and what ought to be avoided is what deserves blame, and Kelsey held firmly to the one and refused the other under heavy pressure.
40._accuracy_note: A clear example of choosing duty and avoiding blameworthy action, though the kural is a general definition rather than a call to resist pressure.
